messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Carlos

Carlos had been driving home from an evening rehearsal when the truck ran the red light. He was fifty-eight then, still dancing professionally—five nights a week at a contemporary theater in the city, his body still responsive, still his own. The collision came from his left side with a sound he could not later describe, though he heard it constantly now: a compressed, metallic shriek that lived somewhere between the car's crumpling frame and his own cry of alarm. The other vehicle had pinned his door, and for the minutes before the fire department arrived, Carlos had been certain he would burn. He remembered the smell of gasoline and hot metal, the weight of the steering wheel against his ribs, and the absolute knowledge that his life was ending—not metaphorically, but in that moment, in that crushed metal box.

He had survived with a fractured collarbone and lacerations across his left shoulder. The physical injuries healed within weeks. What did not heal was the architecture of his certainty about the world. By the time he came to see me, four years had passed, and Carlos had constructed an elaborate system of avoidance and dissociation that had, by his own account, allowed him to continue living—though he was no longer certain that what he was doing constituted life in any meaningful sense.

The first thing Carlos told me was that he believed the collision had happened because of who he was. He had been distracted that evening, replaying a conversation with one of the younger dancers, a moment in which he felt he had been dismissive. He had come to believe that this character flaw—his capacity for selfishness, his aging vanity—had somehow drawn the accident toward him, as if the universe punished moral failing with vehicular catastrophe. This conviction that he was fundamentally unsafe because he was fundamentally flawed had calcified into something unshakeable. From this belief flowed everything else: a constant scanning of his environment for danger, a hypervigilance that had become his baseline. When he entered a room—the studio, a restaurant, his own home—Carlos's eyes moved immediately to exits, calculating routes, assessing which doorways might be blocked. This surveillance was not something he chose; it arose from the deep certainty that bad things happened to people like him, that only constant vigilance might prevent the next catastrophe.

His startle response had become severe enough that his wife, Maria, had stopped touching him without warning. Even her hand on his shoulder from behind could send him into a state of alarm that lasted minutes—his heart racing, his breath shallow, his body rigid. On nights when the hypervigilance felt most acute—when he was scanning exits and cataloging potential threats—the memories would surface unbidden, as if his brain, locked in high alert, needed to keep reviewing the collision to stay ahead of the next catastrophe. The constant scanning kept him tethered to the event itself, pulling the sensory fragments forward into consciousness. She had learned to announce herself, to approach from where he could see her. The shame of this, of flinching from his own wife's affection, only reinforced the darker story he told himself about his nature.

The memories themselves were fragmented and sensory. Carlos could not construct a coherent narrative of the collision; when he tried to speak about it, the words dissolved. What remained were the sounds—that metallic shriek, the hiss of the radiator, the distant wail of sirens—and these would arrive unbidden, sometimes triggered by a car horn or the screech of brakes, sometimes with no apparent cause at all. When the auditory memories surfaced, they would pull him backward into the physical sensation of the crash, and he would find himself dissociating, deliberately leaving his body, floating somewhere above the scene. This dissociation had become his primary refuge. He had learned that if he could blank out sufficiently, if he could achieve a state of profound disconnection from his physical self, the memories would lose their grip. The cost of this strategy was that he had begun to feel increasingly unreal even in ordinary moments—sitting at the dinner table with Maria, teaching a ballet class, lying in bed at night. He had come to believe, with a certainty that terrified him, that he would never feel normal emotions again, that whatever capacity for joy or presence he had once possessed had been burned away in that collision.

To manage the insomnia that accompanied his nighttime hypervigilance, Carlos had begun staying awake until two or three in the morning, reading or sitting in the dark, trying to suppress the intrusive thoughts that came with rest. He would lie beside Maria, exhausted but unable to sleep, and deliberately try not to think about the accident—a strategy that, as he was discovering, only amplified the thoughts' return. His dancing had become impossible. The studio, once a place of joy, had become a space where his body felt like a foreign object, where the mirrors reflected a man he no longer recognized. Six months ago he had stopped performing. He had told his director he needed time, but the truth was that Carlos could no longer trust his body, could no longer feel present enough to dance. The loss of this identity—dancer, artist, someone who moved through the world with grace—had compounded the sense that he was being slowly erased.

It was Maria who finally insisted he seek help. She had watched him disappear into this system of avoidance and dissociation, watched him become a man who flinched at touch and could not sleep and no longer danced. What brought him to my office was not hope, exactly, but exhaustion—the recognition that the strategies that had kept him functioning were now the primary threat to whatever remained of his life.
